qs.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer develops progressive heart failure symptoms. Which antitumor antibiotic is notorious for causing cardiotoxicity requiring monitoring of the ejection fraction?
qs.e: Doxorubicin is an antitumor antibiotic that causes cardiotoxicity, necessitating ejection fraction monitoring and potential cardioprotection with dexrazoxane. Bleomycin is instead associated with pulmonary fibrosis.
qs.s: Master Pharmacokinetics, Dynamics & Antimicrobial Drugs: MCQs

qs.q: An antitumor antibiotic is included in a treatment regimen and is noted for causing unique pulmonary fibrosis as a primary dose-limiting toxicity without significant myelosuppression. What is this drug?
qs.e: Bleomycin generates free radicals causing DNA strand breaks and has a unique toxicity profile featuring pulmonary fibrosis with minimal myelosuppression. Doxorubicin primarily features cardiotoxicity and myelosuppression rather than isolated pulmonary fibrosis.

faq.a: They generate free radicals that damage cardiac myocyte membranes and interfere with topoisomerase‑IIβ, leading to progressive loss of contractile function.
faq.q: Why do anthracyclines cause heart damage?

faq.a: Yes, but monitor closely for neutropenia and drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals.
faq.q: Can antitumor antibiotics be used in patients with HIV?

exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with breast cancer develops new dyspnoea after her third doxorubicin cycle — what bedside assessment and immediate investigations are required? — Assess for signs of heart failure, obtain bedside cardiac ultrasound or ECG, check LVEF; if LVEF <50% stop anthracycline and consider dexrazoxane.

During a chemotherapy cycle a patient presents with fever 38.5 °C and ANC 400 µL — what is the next step and why? — Treat as febrile neutropenia: start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour and admit for monitoring.

You have no echocardiogram available; how can you screen for early anthracycline cardiotoxicity? — Use bedside cardiac ultrasound for gross systolic function, check serum troponin or BNP if possible, and rely on clinical signs of heart failure.

A patient on daunorubicin shows severe mucositis preventing oral intake — how do you manage nutrition and pain? — Initiate IV fluids, analgesia with opioids, consider total parenteral nutrition, and give topical oral agents (lidocaine gel).

Why is cyclophosphamide not interchangeable with doxorubicin in a regimen for acute leukaemia? — Different mechanisms and toxicity profiles; cyclophosphamide causes hemorrhagic cystitis, while doxorubicin carries cardiotoxic risk; regimen efficacy depends on specific drug synergy.
What laboratory result would prompt you to delay the next anthracycline dose? — Grade 3 or 4 neutropenia (ANC <500 µL), LVEF drop >10% to <50%, or ALT/AST >3 × ULN.

In a low‑resource hospital, how would you mitigate cumulative cardiotoxicity without dexrazoxane? — Strict cumulative dose limits, regular clinical cardiac exams, use of liposomal doxorubicin if available, and early referral for echo when possible.

A patient on epirubicin develops a new skin rash and elevated bilirubin — what differential diagnoses should you consider? — Drug‑induced cholestasis, hepatic metastasis, viral hepatitis; order LFTs, hepatitis serology, and abdominal ultrasound.
ai.title: Antitumor Antibiotics
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Antitumor antibiotics are cytotoxic agents that intercalate DNA and generate free radicals, killing rapidly dividing cancer cells. They are used for solid tumours and leukaemias, with specific toxicities that guide monitoring and supportive care, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Key agents: doxorubicin, daunorubicin, epirubicin, idarubicin, mitoxantrone.
sections.p: Antitumor antibiotics are a subclass of cytotoxic chemotherapy that act by intercalating into DNA and producing free‑radical damage, leading to cell death in all phases of the cell cycle.

b: Grade 3–4 neutropenia: ANC <500 µL.
Grade 3–4 cardiotoxicity: LVEF fall >10% to <50%.
sections.p: Toxicity severity is graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) from Grade 1 (mild) to Grade 4 (life‑threatening). Cardiac, hepatic and haematologic toxicities are the most clinically relevant grades.

b: Solid tumours (breast, sarcoma, lung).
Hematologic malignancies (AML, ALL, NHL).
Kaposi sarcoma in HIV‑positive patients.
sections.p: Antitumor antibiotics are prescribed for a range of malignancies; the most common indications in East African hospitals are breast cancer, Kaposi sarcoma, non‑Hodgkin lymphoma and acute leukaemias.

b: Nausea/vomiting within hours of infusion.
Mucositis – painful oral ulcers.
Myelosuppression – bruising, infections.
Cardiotoxicity – dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance.
sections.p: Patients receiving antitumor antibiotics may develop predictable adverse effects that guide bedside assessment.
Baseline and ongoing tests help detect organ toxicity and guide dose adjustments.

t.b: Is the bone marrow suppressed? – Neutrophils <1500 µL indicate need for growth‑factor support or dose delay.
Is hepatic metabolism impaired? – ALT >3 × ULN suggests dose reduction.
Is renal clearance adequate? – eGFR <30 mL/min may require alternative agents.
Is left‑ventricular function preserved? – LVEF <50% or drop >10% from baseline mandates stopping or switching drug.
Can we detect QT prolongation or arrhythmia risk? – QTc >500 ms warrants caution.

b: Febrile neutropenia (temperature ≥38.3 °C with ANC <500 µL).
Acute heart failure – dyspnoea, peripheral oedema, pulmonary crackles.
Severe mucositis causing inability to swallow.
Persistent vomiting leading to electrolyte loss.
sections.p: Early recognition of severe toxicity prevents irreversible damage.

b: Pre‑medication with anti‑emetics (ondansetron, dexamethasone).
Hydration and continuous cardiac monitoring during infusion.
Growth‑factor support (filgrastim) for high‑risk neutropenia.
Dose delay or reduction when CTCAE grade ≥ 3 toxicity occurs.
sections.p: Management combines prevention, early detection and treatment of toxicities while continuing anti‑cancer therapy when safe.

b: Annual skin exam for radiation‑induced sarcoma.
Counselling on infection prevention and nutrition.
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring focuses on cardiac health and secondary malignancies.

b: Alkylating agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide) cause cross‑linking DNA but have different toxicity profiles (hemorrhagic cystitis).
Platinum compounds (cisplatin) cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, not cardiotoxicity.
sections.p: Antitumor antibiotics are sometimes mixed up with other cytotoxics such as alkylating agents or platinum compounds.

b: Normal LVEF early in cardiotoxicity – rely on biomarkers (troponin, BNP) if available.
Transient neutrophil rise after G‑CSF does not guarantee marrow recovery.
sections.p: Certain laboratory values may appear normal despite early organ injury.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute dyspnoea with signs of heart failure
